questions.prompt: A dandelion soaks up sunlight and soil water. A newborn foal drinks its mother's milk. Scientists call sunlight, soil water, and milk resources. What do these three have in common?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A dandelion soaks up sunlight and water from the soil. A newborn foal drinks its mother's milk. Scientists call sunlight, soil water, and milk resources. What do these three things have in common?

choices.text: Each is something an organism needs to live, grow, and reproduce.
choices.rationale: Correct. What makes something a resource is what it does for the organism: the dandelion needs light and water, and the foal needs milk, to stay alive and grow.

choices.text: Each comes from the nonliving part of the organism's environment.
choices.rationale: Milk comes from a living animal, so resources are not only nonliving. Food from living things counts too.

choices.text: Each is made inside the organism's own body, not taken in.
choices.rationale: The dandelion takes in sunlight and water from outside itself, and the foal gets milk from its mother. Resources come from the surroundings.

choices.text: Each is needed only by young organisms that are still growing.
choices.rationale: Adult dandelions and adult horses need resources too. Resources keep organisms alive and let them reproduce, not only grow.

questions.explanation: A resource is any material or energy a living thing needs to survive, grow, and reproduce. Resources can be nonliving, like sunlight and water, or come from living things, like milk or grass. Organisms take them in from their surroundings.
questions.misconception: Resources are only nonliving things, or only things an organism makes for itself.
questions.hint: Think about why the dandelion and the foal each need these things.

questions.prompt: Which of these does a wild horse take from its surroundings to survive and grow? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Which of these things does a wild horse take from its surroundings to survive and grow? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Grass and other plants to eat
choices.rationale: Correct. Plants are a horse's food, a living resource.

choices.text: Water from creeks and ponds
choices.rationale: Correct. Horses drink water from the streams and ponds around them.

choices.text: Oxygen from the air
choices.rationale: Correct. A horse breathes in oxygen from the surrounding air.

choices.text: Sunlight it uses to make its own food
choices.rationale: Horses cannot make food from sunlight; plants do that. A horse gets its food energy by eating plants.

choices.text: Minerals soaked up through roots
choices.rationale: Horses have no roots. Grass takes minerals from the soil through its roots; a horse gets minerals mostly from what it eats.

questions.explanation: A horse eats grass and other plants, drinks from creeks and ponds, and breathes in oxygen. Making food from sunlight and soaking up minerals through roots are how grass gets its resources, not how a horse does.
questions.misconception: Every organism gets its resources the same way, so a horse uses sunlight to make food like a plant.
questions.hint: Check each choice: is it something a horse's body can actually do?

questions.prompt: Wild horses and meadow grass share the same meadow. Which resource does the grass use that a horse does not?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Wild horses and meadow grass live in the same meadow. Which resource does the grass use that a horse does not use?

choices.text: Carbon dioxide, to build its own food
choices.rationale: Correct. Grass takes carbon dioxide from the air and, using light energy, builds food from it. A horse breathes carbon dioxide out as waste and gets its food by eating plants.

choices.text: Water, to keep its cells working
choices.rationale: Both need water: the horse drinks it, and the grass takes it up from the soil.

choices.text: Oxygen, for cellular respiration
choices.rationale: Both use oxygen: the horse breathes it in, and grass cells also use it for cellular respiration, so oxygen is not the difference.

choices.text: Other living things, to eat as its food
choices.rationale: That is backward: the horse eats other living things, but grass makes its own food.

questions.explanation: Grass uses carbon dioxide, water, and light energy to make its own food, and it takes nutrients from the soil. A horse cannot make food, so it eats plants. Both organisms need water. Both also use oxygen, because plant cells and animal cells both carry out cellular respiration.
questions.misconception: Plants and animals use exactly the same gases, or plants use carbon dioxide instead of oxygen.
questions.hint: First rule out anything both the horse and the grass need. Then ask which item only a food-maker needs.

questions.prompt: A cattail plant, a pond snail, and a heron (a wading bird) all live at the same pond. Which statement about their resources is most accurate?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A cattail plant, a pond snail, and a heron, which is a wading bird, all live at the same pond. Which statement about their resources is most accurate?

choices.text: They share some resources, like water, but each needs its own mix.
choices.rationale: Correct. All three need water, but the cattail makes food from sunlight while the snail and heron must eat other living things.

choices.text: They need the same resources, since they share one pond.
choices.rationale: Living in one place does not mean having the same needs. The cattail makes its own food, while the heron must catch animals to eat.

choices.text: The cattail runs on sunlight, while the snail and heron need food and water.
choices.rationale: Plants need more than light: the cattail also takes in water, carbon dioxide, and soil nutrients.

choices.text: Each one gets its food by eating other living things in the pond.
choices.rationale: The snail and heron eat other living things, but the cattail makes its own food using sunlight.

questions.explanation: Organisms that share a habitat often overlap in some needs, such as water and oxygen, but differ in others. A plant builds its own food using sunlight, while animals such as snails and herons must eat other organisms. No single resource recipe fits every living thing.
questions.misconception: Organisms in the same place all need the same resources (one recipe fits all).
questions.hint: Compare how each of the three gets its food.

questions.prompt: A savanna gets far less rain than usual one year. Put these events in cause-and-effect order, from the first cause to the final effect on the zebras.

items.rationale: Last: with fewer survivors and fewer young, the population gets smaller.
Second: grass needs water, so a dry year grows less grass.

items.text: Much less rain falls than usual
items.rationale: First: a change in a nonliving resource, water, starts the chain.

items.text: Zebras that lose out in this competition go hungry, and fewer survive and have young
items.rationale: Fourth: this is the result of the competition in the step before. Zebras that lose out go hungry, and some die or do not reproduce.

items.text: Zebras compete harder for the grass that is left

questions.explanation: A drop in rainfall is the starting cause. Less water means less grass, so zebras compete harder for food. Those that lose out are less likely to survive and reproduce, and the population shrinks. Each link causes the next one.
questions.misconception: A population drops directly because of the weather, or the population shrinks first and the grass declines afterward.
questions.hint: Start with the nonliving change, then follow what each step causes.

questions.prompt: Sort each example of competition: are the competitors members of the same species, or of different species?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort each example of competition into one of two groups: the competitors belong to the same species, or the competitors belong to different species.

items.text: Two wild horses at the last green patch in a dry meadow
items.rationale: Both are wild horses, so this competition is within one species.

items.text: Yaks and wild horses eating grass in one mountain meadow
items.rationale: Yaks and horses are different species that need the same grass.

items.text: Crowded dandelions all drawing on the same soil water
items.rationale: All the plants are dandelions, so they are one species competing for water.

items.text: Zebras and wildebeest grazing the same savanna grass
items.rationale: Zebras and wildebeest are different species sharing one food.

items.text: A growing zebra herd on a shrinking patch of grass
items.rationale: Every member of the herd is a zebra, so the competition is within one species.

items.text: Grass and dandelions in one lawn sharing the same soil water
items.rationale: Grass and dandelions are different species that need the same water.

questions.explanation: Competition can happen inside one species, like horses sharing scarce grass, or between species that need the same resource, like yaks and horses. Either way the shared resource is limited, so what one organism takes is not available to the others.
questions.misconception: Competition only happens between different kinds of organisms, never among members of one species.
questions.hint: Ask whether the competitors are all the same kind of organism.

questions.prompt: Yaks and wild horses graze the same mountain grassland. A dry year leaves much less grass than usual. What do scientists predict will happen?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Yaks and wild horses graze the same mountain grassland. A dry year leaves much less grass than usual. What do scientists predict will happen to the two populations?

choices.text: Both populations will likely shrink as competition for grass grows.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both species depend on the grass, so a shortage raises competition and limits both populations.

choices.text: Only the horses will decline; the yaks will not be affected.
choices.rationale: Yaks depend on grass too. A shortage limits both grazers, not just one.

choices.text: Both populations will grow, since there is less grass to fight over.
choices.rationale: Less grass means more competition, not less. Scarcity limits population growth.

choices.text: Neither will change, since grass is alive and not a resource.
choices.rationale: Living things can be resources. Grass is the food both grazers depend on.

questions.explanation: When two species need the same limited resource, a shortage squeezes both. In a dry year, yaks and horses compete more strongly for grass, so fewer of each survive and reproduce. When grass is plentiful again, competition eases and both populations can grow.
questions.misconception: A resource shortage affects only one of the species that use it, or less food means less competition.
questions.hint: Who eats the grass, and what happens to each eater when there is less of it?

questions.prompt: Yaks often wrap long grass with their tongues, while horses bite grass with front teeth in both jaws and can crop it very short. Suppose each style works best on grass of a different height. How do these feeding styles affect competition between them?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Yaks often wrap long grass with their tongues. Horses bite grass with front teeth in both their upper and lower jaws and can crop it very short. Suppose each style works best on grass of a different height. How do these different feeding styles affect competition between yaks and horses?

choices.text: They reduce competition, which helps both species share a meadow.
choices.rationale: Correct. Using the grass in different ways means they are not always after exactly the same grass, so competition eases and they can coexist.

choices.text: They end competition, so the two species no longer affect each other.
choices.rationale: They still eat grass from the same meadow, so a drought still squeezes both. Feeding differently eases competition but does not end it.

choices.text: They increase competition, because each species eats differently.
choices.rationale: Eating differently spreads the two species across different parts of the resource, which lowers competition rather than raising it.

choices.text: They change nothing, because different species never compete.
choices.rationale: Different species compete whenever they need the same limited resource, as yaks and horses do.

questions.explanation: When competing species use a shared resource in slightly different ways, each does best under somewhat different conditions, such as taller or shorter grass. That lowers the overlap between them, which reduces competition and lets them live side by side. It eases competition; it does not erase it.
questions.misconception: Feeding differently removes competition completely, or different species never compete.
questions.hint: Picture the meadow: which grass would each grazer go for first, and how often would they want the same patch?

questions.prompt: A mountain meadow grows enough grass in one season to feed 40 wild horses. A herd of yaks moves in and eats one-fourth of that grass. If each horse still needs the same amount, how many horses can the rest of the grass feed?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A mountain meadow grows enough grass in one season to feed 40 wild horses. A herd of yaks moves in and eats one fourth of that grass. If each horse still needs the same amount of grass, how many horses can the remaining grass feed?
questions.conditions: Grass is the only limited resource in this model, the meadow grows the same amount as before, and every horse eats the same amount.
questions.limitations: A simplified model: real herds also depend on water, weather, predators, and how each species feeds.
questions.workedSolution: The yaks eat 1/4 of the grass, so 3/4 is left. 3/4 × 40 horses = 30 horses. Competition from the yaks lowers the number of horses the meadow can feed from 40 to 30.
questions.explanation: Every mouthful a yak eats is grass a horse cannot have. When another species takes a share of a limited resource, less remains for the first population, so the area can support fewer of its members.
questions.misconception: Another species eating the same food does not change how many horses an area can support.
questions.hint: If one-fourth of the grass is gone, what fraction is left for the horses?

questions.prompt: A population of animals depends on one main food. What may happen to that population if its food supply decreases?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A population of animals depends on one main food. What may happen to that population if its food supply gets smaller?

choices.text: Its growth may be limited, or it may decline, depending on conditions.
choices.rationale: Correct. Less food means fewer animals get enough to survive and reproduce, but the exact result also depends on things like water, weather, and other foods.

choices.text: It keeps growing at the same rate, because each animal simply eats a bit less.
choices.rationale: Animals that get too little food may not survive or reproduce, so growth does not simply carry on unchanged.

choices.text: It dies out completely within a year.
choices.rationale: A smaller food supply limits a population, but how far it falls depends on conditions such as other foods and water. A total die-off is not the expected result.

choices.text: It grows faster, because hungry animals tend to have more young.
choices.rationale: Underfed animals are less likely to survive and reproduce, so a food shortage usually holds a population down, not up.

questions.explanation: A population can only grow as large as its resources allow. When a needed food becomes scarcer, competition rises, fewer individuals get enough to survive and reproduce, and the population's growth may be limited or the population may decline. How much depends on other conditions, such as other foods, water, and weather.
questions.misconception: Population size does not depend on food supply, or a food shortage always wipes a population out.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the share of food each animal gets.

questions.prompt: Zebras on a savanna all eat the same grass. Which changes would most likely make the zebras compete harder for food? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Zebras on a savanna all eat the same grass. Which changes would most likely make the zebras compete harder for food? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A drought year leaves far less grass than usual
choices.rationale: Correct. Less grass for the same number of zebras means harder competition.

choices.text: A large herd of wildebeest arrives and eats the same grass
choices.rationale: Correct. Another species taking a share leaves less grass for each zebra.

choices.text: The zebra herd doubles while the grass stays the same
choices.rationale: Correct. Twice as many zebras sharing the same grass means each gets less.

choices.text: Heavy rains make the grass grow thick and tall all season
choices.rationale: More grass means each zebra can find enough more easily, so competition eases.

choices.text: Half of the zebras move away to settle in another valley
choices.rationale: Fewer zebras sharing the same grass means less competition among those that stay.

questions.explanation: Competition gets stronger whenever there is less of a limited resource for each individual. That happens when the resource shrinks (a drought), when another species takes a share (wildebeest), or when more individuals need it (a bigger herd).
questions.misconception: Competition depends only on how many zebras there are, not on how much grass there is or who else eats it.
questions.hint: For each change, ask: does each zebra end up with more grass or less?

questions.prompt: After several very rainy years, a valley grows three times as much grass as before, and its wild horse population starts to grow. Which prediction about the next several years is most reasonable?

choices.text: It grows until grass, water, or space limits it again.

Rooted plants can grow deeper in the clear lake, where enough light still reaches the bottom.
questions.misconception: Plants underwater don't depend on light, or light reaches all depths equally.
questions.hint: Plants can only grow where enough light reaches them.

questions.prompt: Put these levels of organization in order, from the smallest to the largest.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Put four levels of organization, biosphere, population, organism, and ecosystem, in order from the smallest level to the largest level.
questions.limitations: Uses the four levels taught in this lesson; many biology books also add a community level between population and ecosystem.

items.rationale: Largest: all of Earth's ecosystems together.
Second: many organisms of one species living in one area.
Smallest level here: one individual living thing.
Third: populations plus the nonliving parts of their environment.

questions.explanation: Each level contains the one before it. Organisms of one species living in an area form a population; populations plus the nonliving parts around them form an ecosystem; and all of Earth's ecosystems together form the biosphere.
questions.misconception: An ecosystem is smaller than a population, or the biosphere is just the air around Earth.
questions.hint: Start with one living thing and keep zooming out.

questions.explanation: Look at what each description includes. One living thing is an organism. Many of one species in an area make a population. questions.prompt: Which human actions would leave less grass for wild horses on a grassland? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Which human actions would leave less grass for wild horses living on a grassland? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Grazing large herds of sheep and goats on the same land
choices.rationale: Correct. Livestock eat the same grass, adding competition for the wild horses.

choices.text: Plowing the grassland to plant crops
choices.rationale: Correct. Turning grassland into farmland removes the horses' food and shrinks the ecosystem.

choices.text: Building neighborhoods across the grassland
choices.rationale: Correct. Houses and roads replace grass, so the grassland ecosystem shrinks.

choices.text: Fencing livestock out of a protected grassland reserve
choices.rationale: Keeping livestock out lowers competition, leaving more grass for wild horses.

choices.text: Capturing some wild horses to tame them
choices.rationale: This lowers the number of wild horses, but it removes no grass, so the horses that stay wild are not left with less to eat.

questions.explanation: Humans are part of ecosystems and use their resources. Grazing livestock adds competition for grass, and turning grassland into farms or neighborhoods shrinks the ecosystem itself. Either way, less grass is left for wild species.
questions.misconception: Humans stand outside ecosystems, so their land use doesn't affect wild populations.
questions.hint: For each action, ask whether it uses up grass or replaces grassland.

evidence.locator: Section 5. Organization of Earth's Biosphere (human impacts)
evidence.supports: Humans grazed livestock on grasslands, adding competition for grass, and turned grasslands into farms and neighborhoods; using food and water leaves less for other species, whose decline changes the ecosystem.

questions.prompt: A growing city starts pumping much more water out of a river for its homes and farms. Which prediction best fits what you know about resources and ecosystems?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A growing city starts pumping much more water out of a river for its homes and farms. Which prediction best fits what you know about resources and ecosystems?

choices.text: Some river populations may shrink, changing the ecosystem.
choices.rationale: Correct. Taking water reduces what other species can use; populations that need it may shrink, changing the ecosystem.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because people are not part of ecosystems.
choices.rationale: People use resources from ecosystems, even in cities, so their use affects other species.

choices.text: Every population in the river will die out right away.
choices.rationale: Effects depend on how much water is taken and how each species copes; a sudden total loss is not a sure thing.

choices.text: The city's people will feel the effects, but the river's wildlife will not.
choices.rationale: Fish, plants, and other river species need that water too. When the city takes more, less is left for them.

questions.explanation: When people use a resource, less of it remains for other species. As populations that need that water decline, the whole ecosystem changes. How large the effect is depends on how much water is taken and on other conditions.
questions.misconception: Human resource use has no effect on wild populations, or it always wipes them out completely.
questions.hint: Who else in the ecosystem needs that river water?
